category.name: Java Interview Prep
category.description: Java 8 to 21 interview preparation: concepts, output-prediction questions and mock tests

subjects.name: Java 8 Essentials
subjects.description: Lambdas, streams, collectors, Optional, default methods and java.time

questions.q: What makes an interface a functional interface?
options: It has no methods at all
It has exactly one abstract method
questions.why: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method; default and static methods do not count. @FunctionalInterface is optional: it only makes the compiler enforce the rule.

questions.q: Which built-in functional interface converts a value of type T into a value of type R?
questions.why: Function<T, R> has apply(T) returning R. Predicate returns boolean, Consumer returns nothing, Supplier takes no input.

questions.q: What does Predicate<T>.test(t) return?
questions.why: A Predicate is a yes/no test, so test() returns a primitive boolean. It is what filter() expects.

questions.q: Inside a lambda expression, what does `this` refer to?
options: The thread that runs the lambda
questions.why: A lambda does not introduce a new scope for this. In an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object, which is a key difference.

questions.q: What happens when this code is compiled?
options: Compile error: a local variable used in a lambda must be final or effectively final
It compiles but throws an exception at runtime
count ends up equal to list.size()
questions.why: Lambdas capture a copy of local variables, so they must never be reassigned. Use an array, an AtomicInteger, or a stream operation such as count() instead.

questions.q: Which comparator sorts employees by salary descending and breaks ties by name ascending?
questions.why: reversed() applies to the comparator built so far (salary), then thenComparing adds the name tie-break. Putting reversed() last would reverse the name order too.

questions.q: Which statement about @FunctionalInterface is correct?
options: It is required for a lambda to be assigned to the interface
It is optional; it makes the compiler reject the interface if it gets a second abstract method
questions.why: Any interface with one abstract method can be the target of a lambda. The annotation just documents the intent and adds a compile-time check.

questions.q: Comparator declares equals(Object) as an abstract method, yet it is a functional interface. Why?
options: equals is a default method in Comparator
The compiler ignores the first abstract method
Methods that match public methods of Object do not count as abstract methods for this purpose
Comparator is a class, not an interface
questions.why: Every class already inherits equals from Object, so an interface redeclaring it does not add a method an implementer must write.

questions.q: How are lambdas compiled compared with anonymous classes?
options: Each lambda generates its own .class file, like an anonymous class
Lambdas are converted to inner enums at compile time
Lambdas use invokedynamic and do not produce a separate .class file for each lambda
Lambdas are only evaluated at class-loading time
questions.why: The compiler emits an invokedynamic call and the JVM creates the implementation at runtime, which avoids a class file per lambda.

topics.name: Stream Basics
topics.description: Stream pipelines, terminal and intermediate operations

questions.q: Which of these is a terminal stream operation?
questions.why: Terminal operations such as count(), collect(), forEach() and findFirst() start the pipeline. filter, map and sorted are intermediate and lazy.

questions.q: What happens if you call a terminal operation on a stream that has already been consumed?
options: The stream restarts from the beginning
questions.why: A stream can be traversed only once. Create a new stream from the source if you need another pass.

questions.q: What does this code print?
options: Nothing, because there is no terminal operation
Lowercase a, b, c on separate lines
Uppercase A, B, C on separate lines
questions.why: Intermediate operations are lazy. Without a terminal operation the pipeline never runs, so peek() prints nothing.

questions.q: What does this expression return?
questions.why: Elements flow one at a time: 1 fails the filter, 2 passes and becomes 4, and findFirst() stops the whole pipeline. The result is wrapped in an Optional.

questions.q: Which pipeline returns the second-highest distinct salary?
questions.why: distinct() must come first. Without it, a duplicated top salary would be returned as the "second highest".

questions.q: What does allMatch(...) return on an empty stream?
questions.why: allMatch is vacuously true when there is no element to violate the predicate. anyMatch is false and noneMatch is true on an empty stream.

questions.q: What is n?
questions.why: Stream.of(int[]) treats the whole array as a single element (a Stream<int[]>). Use Arrays.stream(arr) or IntStream.of(arr) to stream the numbers.

questions.q: What does IntStream.range(1, 5).sum() return?
questions.why: range excludes the end value, so it sums 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. rangeClosed(1, 5) would give 15.

questions.q: What is the return type of Stream.count()?
questions.why: count() returns a primitive long, so compare with 3L or cast when you need an int.

topics.name: Collectors
topics.description: groupingBy, partitioningBy, toMap, summarizing and more

questions.q: What is the type of emps.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDept, Collectors.counting()))?
questions.why: groupingBy keys by the classifier result (the department name) and counting() produces a Long per group.

questions.q: How does Collectors.partitioningBy differ from groupingBy?
options: It sorts the elements before grouping
It always produces exactly two groups, keyed true and false
It returns a Set instead of a Map
It can only be used on numeric streams
questions.why: partitioningBy takes a predicate and the resulting map always has both a true and a false key, even if one group is empty.

questions.q: What happens when Collectors.toMap(keyFn, valueFn) meets a duplicate key?
options: IllegalStateException is thrown unless a merge function is supplied
questions.why: Use the three-argument form, for example toMap(k, v, Integer::sum), to say how duplicates are combined.

questions.q: Which collector returns count, sum, min, average and max in a single pass?
questions.why: summarizingInt/Long/Double return an IntSummaryStatistics-style object with getCount, getSum, getMin, getAverage and getMax.

questions.q: How do you make groupingBy return its keys in sorted order?
options: groupingBy always returns a sorted map
Pass TreeMap::new as the map factory: groupingBy(f, TreeMap::new, downstream)
questions.why: The default result is a HashMap with no ordering guarantee. The three-argument groupingBy lets you choose TreeMap or LinkedHashMap.

questions.q: What is the result type of Collectors.counting()?
questions.why: counting() produces a Long. That is why comparisons such as entry.getValue() > 1 work but equals(1) would not match a Long.

questions.q: What happens if a value is null in Collectors.toMap(...)?
options: The entry is stored with a null value
questions.why: toMap is built on HashMap.merge, which rejects null values. Filter nulls first or use a different collector.

questions.q: What does Collectors.teeing (Java 12) do?
options: Splits a stream into two streams
Runs two collectors over the same stream in one pass and merges their results
Collects into two lists without merging
Runs the pipeline on two threads
questions.why: For example teeing(minBy, maxBy, (min, max) -> ...) computes both in a single traversal.

questions.q: Which statement about reduce and collect is correct?
options: reduce combines elements into an immutable value; collect accumulates into a mutable container
collect is only for parallel streams
questions.why: reduce is immutable reduction (for example summing). collect is mutable reduction (filling a list, map or StringBuilder).

topics.name: flatMap & Laziness
topics.description: flatMap, distinct, skip, limit and evaluation order

questions.q: What is the difference between map and flatMap on a Stream?
options: flatMap is the lazy version of map
map works on collections and flatMap works on arrays
map is one-to-one; flatMap maps each element to a stream and flattens the results
questions.why: Use flatMap when each element produces zero or more results, such as the words in a sentence.

questions.q: If nested is a List<List<Integer>>, what is the type of nested.stream().flatMap(List::stream)?
questions.why: flatMap replaces each inner list with its elements and concatenates them into one Stream<Integer>.

questions.q: What is printed by this pipeline (no sorted)?
questions.why: Elements travel through the whole pipeline one at a time, so the peek and forEach outputs interleave.

questions.q: What is printed by this pipeline (with sorted)?
questions.why: sorted() is a stateful barrier: it must see every element before emitting the first one, so all peek output comes first.

questions.q: What does IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).skip(3).limit(3) produce?
questions.why: skip(3) drops 1, 2, 3 and limit(3) keeps the next three values. This is the pagination pattern: skip((page - 1) * size).limit(size).

questions.q: Which two stream operations are stateful?
questions.why: Stateful operations may need to remember or buffer elements. filter and map handle each element independently.

questions.q: How do you find the third-highest DISTINCT number in a List<Integer>?
questions.why: Deduplicate, sort descending, skip the top two and take the next. The result is an Optional because the list may have fewer than three distinct values.

questions.q: Why is the (long) cast used in skip((long) (page - 1) * size)?
options: Because skip only accepts negative numbers
To avoid int overflow when the page offset is large
Because limit requires a long start index
questions.why: skip() takes a long. Multiplying two ints first could overflow before the value is widened, so cast one operand to long.

questions.q: What does "abc".chars() return?
questions.why: chars() returns an IntStream. Convert with mapToObj(c -> (char) c) when you need Character objects.

questions.q: Why use a LinkedHashMap when finding the first non-repeating character with streams?
options: It keeps first-seen order so the first entry with count 1 is the answer
questions.why: A HashMap has no ordering guarantee. LinkedHashMap preserves the order characters first appeared.

questions.q: What is n when counting the letter s in "swiss"?
questions.why: chars() yields the code units of "swiss"; the letter s appears three times (s, w, i, s, s) and count() returns 3.

questions.q: What is n when "a  b" (two spaces) is split on a single space?
questions.why: split(" ") on a string with two consecutive spaces produces an empty string between them: ["a", "", "b"]. Use split("\\s+") to avoid that.

questions.q: How can you check whether two strings are anagrams using streams?
options: Use distinct() on both and compare the sizes
Sort the characters of both strings and compare the results
questions.why: Anagrams have identical sorted character sequences: Arrays.equals(a.chars().sorted().toArray(), b.chars().sorted().toArray()).

questions.q: Which characters of "programming" appear more than once?
questions.why: In p-r-o-g-r-a-m-m-i-n-g the letters r, g and m each occur twice.

questions.q: Which method correctly streams code points, including emoji outside the Basic Multilingual Plane?
questions.why: chars() returns UTF-16 code units, so a supplementary character appears as two surrogate halves. codePoints() returns whole characters.

questions.q: Why should you compare two Long objects, such as map values, with equals instead of ==?
options: == compares references, and Long values outside the small cache range are different objects
== is not allowed for wrapper types
questions.why: Long.valueOf caches -128 to 127, so 100L == 100L can be true while 1000L == 1000L is false. A comparison like value == 1 against an int literal unboxes and is fine.

topics.name: Optional & Method References
topics.description: Optional API and the four kinds of method reference

questions.q: What does Optional.of(null) do?
questions.why: of() requires a non-null value. Use ofNullable() when the value may be null.

questions.q: What does Optional.ofNullable(null) return?
questions.why: ofNullable wraps a value that may be null: null becomes Optional.empty().

questions.q: What is the difference between orElse(x) and orElseGet(supplier)?
options: orElse is lazy; orElseGet is eager
orElse always evaluates its argument; orElseGet calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty
orElseGet throws if the Optional is present
questions.why: orElse(expensive()) runs expensive() even when a value is present. orElseGet(() -> expensive()) skips it.

questions.q: user.getEmail() returns Optional<String>. Which call gives an Optional<String> without nesting?
questions.why: map would produce Optional<Optional<String>>. flatMap is for functions that already return an Optional.

questions.q: What kind of method reference is String::toUpperCase?
questions.why: The receiver is supplied later as the first argument: s -> s.toUpperCase().

questions.q: What kind of method reference is System.out::println?
questions.why: The receiver (System.out) is fixed when the reference is created: x -> System.out.println(x).

questions.q: What kind of method reference is User::new?
questions.why: User::new calls a constructor, for example name -> new User(name). ArrayList::new and String[]::new work the same way.

questions.q: Why is Optional a poor choice for a class field or method parameter?
options: It only works with primitive types
It is not allowed by the compiler
It adds allocation and noise, is not Serializable, and does not stop callers passing null for the Optional itself
questions.why: Optional is designed for return types that may have no value. For fields and parameters, plain nullable values or overloads are clearer.

questions.q: What does calling get() on an empty Optional throw?
questions.why: Prefer orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow or ifPresent. Since Java 10, orElseThrow() with no argument is the clear replacement for get().

questions.q: Why were default methods added to interfaces in Java 8?
options: So interfaces can gain new methods without breaking existing implementations
To allow multiple inheritance of state
questions.why: This is how Collection.stream(), List.sort() and Iterable.forEach were added without breaking every existing class.

questions.q: Class Duck implements two interfaces that both define a default method move(). What must Duck do?
options: Declare move() final in both interfaces
Override move() and, if needed, call Walker.super.move() or Swimmer.super.move()
Nothing; the compiler picks the alphabetically first
questions.why: This is the diamond problem. The compiler reports an error until the class overrides the method and chooses explicitly.

questions.q: Are static methods declared in an interface inherited by implementing classes?
options: No; they must be called on the interface name
Only when the class also overrides them
Yes, but only if the interface is public
questions.why: Static interface methods belong to the interface alone: Shape.square(3), not an instance or implementing class.

questions.q: What does LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1) return?
questions.why: When the day does not exist in the target month, java.time clamps to the last valid day of that month.

questions.q: What is the difference between Period and Duration?
options: Period is mutable; Duration is immutable
Period is date-based (years, months, days); Duration is time-based (hours, minutes, seconds)
Period is for time zones; Duration is for leap years
questions.why: Period.between takes two dates. Duration.between takes two times or instants.

questions.q: In a DateTimeFormatter pattern, what does mm stand for?
questions.why: Lower-case mm is minutes and upper-case MM is the month number. MMM gives the month name.

questions.q: What does ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1), LocalDate.of(2026, 3, 1)) return?
questions.why: January has 31 days and February 2026 has 28 (2026 is not a leap year), so 31 + 28 = 59.

questions.q: Why is java.time preferred over Date and SimpleDateFormat?
options: java.time types are immutable and thread-safe, while SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe
java.time is faster only on Linux
questions.why: DateTimeFormatter and the java.time value types can be shared freely between threads. SimpleDateFormat has mutable internal state.

subjects.name: Modern Java (9 to 21)
subjects.description: Features added from Java 9 to the Java 21 LTS release

topics.name: Java 9 & 10
topics.description: List.of, takeWhile, private interface methods, var

questions.q: What does List.of(1, 2, 3).add(4) do?
questions.why: List.of returns an immutable list.

questions.q: Where can var be used?
questions.why: var is local-variable type inference. It does not make Java dynamically typed: the type is still fixed at compile time.

questions.q: What does List.of(1, null) do?
options: Creates a list with a null element
Creates a list and ignores the null
questions.why: The List.of family rejects nulls. Arrays.asList(1, null) is allowed.

questions.q: Which elements remain after takeWhile(n -> n < 5)?
questions.why: takeWhile stops at the first element that fails the predicate (10), so the trailing 1 is not included. filter would keep both 1s.

questions.q: Which elements remain after dropWhile(n -> n < 5)?
questions.why: dropWhile discards elements while the predicate holds and then keeps everything that follows, including the trailing 1.

questions.q: How does List.copyOf(list) differ from Collections.unmodifiableList(list)?
options: copyOf returns a view; unmodifiableList returns a copy
copyOf makes an immutable snapshot; unmodifiableList is a read-only view that changes when the source changes
questions.why: Changing the original list shows through an unmodifiable view but never through a copyOf snapshot.

questions.q: Which Java version added private methods in interfaces?
questions.why: Private interface methods let default methods share code without exposing a helper.

questions.q: What does Map.of("a", 1, "a", 2) do?
options: Throws IllegalArgumentException because of the duplicate key
questions.why: Map.of and Set.of reject duplicates at creation time. Their iteration order is also unspecified.

topics.name: Java 11 & 12
topics.description: String methods, Files, teeing, single-file launch

questions.q: What does " ".isBlank() return?
questions.why: isBlank() is true for empty or whitespace-only strings. isEmpty() is true only for length 0.

questions.q: What does "ab".repeat(3) return?
questions.why: repeat(n) concatenates the string n times.

questions.q: How does String.strip() differ from trim()?
options: trim() is Unicode-aware; strip() is not
strip() removes all Unicode whitespace; trim() removes only characters up to U+0020
questions.why: Text copied from web pages often contains non-ASCII spaces that trim() leaves behind.

questions.q: In which Java version was Collectors.teeing added?
questions.why: teeing runs two collectors in one pass and combines their results.

questions.q: What is Predicate.not(String::isBlank) used for?
options: Converting a Predicate to a Function
Creating a Predicate that always returns false
Negating a method reference, for example keeping only non-blank strings in a filter
questions.why: It replaces s -> !s.isBlank() with a cleaner reference: lines.filter(Predicate.not(String::isBlank)).

questions.q: Which charset do Files.readString(path) and Files.writeString(path, text) use by default?
questions.why: Both methods default to UTF-8 and load the whole file into memory.

questions.q: How can you run a single-file Java program in Java 11 without a separate javac step?
questions.why: The source-file launcher compiles in memory and runs the file.

questions.q: What does "a\nb".indent(2) produce?
options: Two blank lines added before the text
The text unchanged; indent only works on text blocks
Both lines indented by two spaces, with a trailing newline added
Only the first line indented by two spaces
questions.why: indent(n) adds n leading spaces to every line, normalizes line endings and ends the result with a newline.

topics.name: Java 14 to 16
topics.description: Switch expressions, text blocks, records, pattern instanceof

questions.q: What is the accessor for a record component named name?
questions.why: Record accessors use the component name, not JavaBean-style getters.

questions.q: In a switch expression that uses ->, what happens after a case matches?
options: No fall-through; only that case runs
The switch exits only if break is used
Execution falls through to the next case
questions.why: Arrow cases never fall through and the switch expression produces a value.

questions.q: What is r?
questions.why: case 3 runs the block and yield returns t * 3 = 15.

questions.q: Can a record extend another class?
options: No; records are implicitly final and extend java.lang.Record, but they can implement interfaces
Only if it is declared sealed
questions.why: A record is a transparent immutable data carrier, so it cannot have a superclass other than Record.

questions.q: What does Stream.toList() (Java 16) return?
questions.why: Unlike Collectors.toList(), toList() guarantees an unmodifiable list and allows null elements.

questions.q: In a text block, what determines how much indentation is stripped?
options: The least-indented content line, including the closing delimiter
questions.why: Moving the closing triple quotes left or right changes the indentation of the whole block.

questions.q: What does if (o instanceof String s && !s.isEmpty()) give you?
options: A compile error; the cast must be explicit
A variable s of type Object
A pattern variable s, already cast to String, usable in the rest of the condition and the true branch
questions.why: Pattern matching for instanceof (final in Java 16) removes the separate cast.

questions.q: Why is record Person(List<String> tags) only shallowly immutable?
options: The reference to the list is final, but the list itself can still be modified
questions.why: Make a defensive copy (List.copyOf) in a compact constructor if you need deep immutability.

topics.name: Java 17: Sealed Classes
topics.description: Sealed classes, permits, non-sealed, Java 17 changes

questions.q: What does the permits clause of a sealed class do?
options: Lists the only classes allowed to extend or implement it directly
Lists the classes it is forbidden to extend
questions.why: A sealed hierarchy is closed: the compiler and readers know every direct subtype.

questions.q: Which modifiers can a direct subclass of a sealed class have?
questions.why: Records and enums are implicitly final, so they satisfy the rule automatically.

questions.q: When can the permits clause be omitted?
options: When the subclasses are in another module
When the permitted subclasses are in the same source file
questions.why: The compiler infers the permitted subclasses declared in the same compilation unit.

questions.q: What common effect does Java 17's strong encapsulation of JDK internals have on old applications?
options: Reflective access to JDK internals fails unless opened with --add-opens
questions.why: This is why upgrading from Java 8 or 11 to 17 often exposes libraries that rely on illegal reflective access.

questions.q: What was the status of pattern matching for switch in Java 17?
questions.why: Java 17 finalized sealed classes, but switch patterns stayed in preview until Java 21.

questions.q: Which method returns the permitted subclasses of a sealed type at runtime?
questions.why: Class.isSealed() tells you whether a type is sealed.

questions.q: What does marking a permitted subclass non-sealed do?
options: Reopens the hierarchy below it, so anyone may extend that subclass
questions.why: Use it deliberately where you want extension beyond the closed set.

questions.q: Which list contains only long-term support (LTS) releases?
questions.why: LTS releases get years of updates. Java 25 is the latest LTS after 21.

topics.name: Java 21
topics.description: Virtual threads, pattern switch, record patterns, sequenced collections

questions.q: What is the status of virtual threads in Java 21?
questions.why: Virtual threads were previewed in Java 19 and 20 and finalized in Java 21.

questions.q: Which method returns the last element of a List in Java 21?
questions.why: List now implements SequencedCollection, which adds getFirst(), getLast(), reversed() and more.

questions.q: Should you pool virtual threads in a fixed-size thread pool?
options: No; create one per task because they are cheap
Yes, always cap them at the number of CPU cores
questions.why: Use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() and limit concurrency with a Semaphore if needed.

questions.q: Virtual threads help most with:
options: Reducing the heap usage of a single task
Many concurrent tasks that spend their time blocked on I/O
questions.why: A blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier thread, letting the carrier run other work.

questions.q: What is this syntax called?
questions.why: Record patterns deconstruct a record in switch or instanceof and were finalized in Java 21.
questions.code: case Circle(double r) -> Math.PI * r * r;

questions.q: In a pattern switch, where must case Integer i when i > 10 appear relative to case Integer i?
options: Before it; otherwise the guarded case is dominated and does not compile
questions.why: The compiler rejects a case that an earlier, more general case would always catch.

questions.q: In Java 21, what is thread pinning?
options: A virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block stays attached to its carrier thread, reducing scalability
Assigning a thread to a CPU core
Pausing the JVM for garbage collection
questions.why: Prefer ReentrantLock over synchronized around blocking calls when using virtual threads on Java 21.

questions.q: What was the status of string templates in Java 21?
questions.why: Do not rely on preview features in production code.

questions.q: Which CompletableFuture method is the equivalent of Stream.map?
questions.why: thenApply transforms the result. thenCompose is the flatMap equivalent.

questions.q: How do join() and get() differ?
options: get() is only for completed futures
join() throws the unchecked CompletionException; get() throws the checked ExecutionException and InterruptedException
questions.why: join() is convenient inside lambdas because it needs no try/catch.

questions.q: When should you use thenCompose instead of thenApply?
options: When running on a custom executor
When the next step returns void
When the next step itself returns a CompletableFuture
questions.why: thenApply would give CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>. thenCompose flattens it.

questions.q: Which pool does supplyAsync(supplier) use by default?
questions.why: Pass your own Executor for blocking or I/O-heavy tasks.

questions.q: What does CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2) return?
options: CompletableFuture<Void>; you read the values from f1 and f2 yourself
questions.why: Call join() on allOf to wait, then join() each individual future for its value.

questions.q: An exception is thrown inside supplyAsync. What does handle((v, ex) -> ...) receive as ex?
options: A CompletionException wrapping the original exception
questions.why: Use ex.getCause() to reach the original exception. This was verified by running the code on a JDK.

questions.q: What does parallelStream().forEach(...) guarantee about order?
options: No order guarantee; use forEachOrdered if order matters
questions.why: collect(toList()) preserves encounter order, but forEach does not on a parallel stream.

questions.q: When is parallelStream() a bad choice?
options: Summing a big range of numbers
Small data, blocking I/O inside the lambda, or shared mutable state
questions.why: Parallel streams use the common pool, so blocking tasks can starve unrelated work.
